Between 1974 and 1986, one man broke into homes across California. At least thirteen murders. Around fifty sexual assaults. More than a hundred burglaries. DNA proved it was all one man, but he was in no database. The case went cold for decades. Then, in 2018, investigators tried something nobody had tried before.

This is the case of the Golden State Killer. Part two.

In this episode, we follow one sample of DNA, from a 40-year-old crime scene to the handle of a car door.

And the question is simple.

How do you find a killer whose name is in no file, whose face nobody saw, and who stopped forty years ago?

By 2017, a small team of investigators had taken over the old files. One of them was a cold case investigator named Paul Holes, who had worked the case for most of his career and was close to retiring.

They had the killer's DNA. What they needed was a name.

So they turned to a new idea: genealogy websites.

Millions of people had sent their DNA to companies to learn about their ancestry. Some of them uploaded their results to a free public website called GEDmatch, to find long-lost relatives.

The investigators created a profile from the killer's DNA and uploaded it.

They weren't looking for the killer himself. They were looking for his cousins.

It was a legal grey area. Nobody had ever caught a serial killer this way before. And there was no guarantee it would work.

The results came back. No close family. But distant relatives. Third cousins. Fourth cousins.

People who shared a tiny amount of DNA with the killer, through great-great-grandparents who lived more than a century ago.

A genealogist, Barbara Rae-Venter, helped the team build family trees backwards, generation by generation. Then forwards again, through every branch, every marriage, every child.

They ended up with thousands of names.

Then they started crossing people out. Women. People too young or too old. People who never lived in California.

Slowly, the list shrank.

The method wasn't perfect. In 2017, an earlier family search had pointed to a different man, an elderly man in Oregon. Investigators obtained his DNA.

He was innocent. The trail went cold again.

This time, they had to be certain.

One name kept surviving every filter.

A man born in 1945. The right age. He had lived in the Central Valley in the 1970s, when the Visalia Ransacker struck. He had lived near Sacramento when the East Area Rapist struck. He had family connections to Southern California.

And he had been a police officer.

Joseph James DeAngelo. Now 72 years old. Retired. Living in Citrus Heights, a short drive from the neighbourhoods he had terrorised.

But a name in a family tree isn't proof. It's a lead. Investigators needed his DNA.

And they couldn't ask for it without warning him.

So they watched him.

On April 18, 2018, DeAngelo drove to a Hobby Lobby craft store in Roseville. He parked and went inside.

While he shopped, investigators walked up to his car and swabbed the handle of the driver's door.

The sample went to the crime lab of the Sacramento County District Attorney.

It was a likely match.

To be sure, they needed something better. On the night of April 23, they went through the bin outside his house. Among the rubbish, they found a used tissue.

The lab tested it.

It matched the Golden State Killer.

Decades of evidence, from Visalia to Sacramento to the Southern California coast, all pointed to one man, sitting in a quiet house in the suburbs.

The next day, April 24, 2018, officers surrounded the house in Citrus Heights.

DeAngelo walked out of his front door. They arrested him on the spot.

According to reports from the time, he told the officers he had a roast in the oven.

Forty-two years after the first attack in Sacramento, the man in the mask had a name.

The next morning, at a press conference, the Sacramento District Attorney, Anne Marie Schubert, announced the arrest. Survivors who had waited four decades watched on television.

Some of them said they had stopped believing this day would come.

In the interview room after his arrest, according to prosecutors, DeAngelo talked to himself for hours. He spoke about another personality he called "Jerry", who, he said, had made him do it.

Prosecutors later said he made a statement that amounted to a confession: "I did all that."

Then came the question everyone was asking. How?

How could a police officer commit these crimes while wearing a badge? How could a man live next door to people for thirty years without anyone noticing?

Neighbours described him as short-tempered. Some remembered him yelling and swearing. But nobody imagined this.

His former police chief in Auburn later said he was an average cop.

Investigators believe his police training helped him. He knew how investigations worked. He knew how to avoid leaving evidence. He knew how long police would take to respond.

But it didn't protect him from the one thing he couldn't control.

His own DNA, sitting in his relatives' family trees.

In 2020, the case went to court. Because of the pandemic, it took place in an unusual setting: a large ballroom at California State University, Sacramento, with everyone spread apart.

DeAngelo arrived in a wheelchair. He looked frail. He spoke in a weak voice.

Prosecutors had wanted the death penalty. Instead, they agreed to a deal. Given his age, the ages of many witnesses, and California's pause on executions, they accepted guilty pleas in exchange for life in prison.

On June 29, 2020, Joseph James DeAngelo pleaded guilty to thirteen murders, starting with Claude Snelling in Visalia in 1975, and thirteen kidnapping-related charges.

He also admitted dozens of other attacks that were too old to be charged.

Prosecutors said there were 87 victims, at 53 crime scenes, in 11 California counties.

In August 2020, before the sentence, the court gave the victims a voice.

For several days, survivors and families stood up, one by one, and spoke directly to him.

They talked about the decades of fear. Locks on every window. Lights left on at night. Marriages that broke apart. Children who grew up afraid of the dark.

Some called him a coward. Some said they forgave him. Many said that, for the first time in forty years, they were no longer afraid.

At the end, DeAngelo stood up and spoke briefly. He said he was truly sorry to everyone he had hurt.

On August 21, 2020, the judge sentenced him to eleven consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole, plus more terms for the other crimes.

He will die in prison.

Survivors said what they felt most was not anger, but relief. For decades, they had wondered if the man was still out there. Now they knew exactly where he was.

The arrest of the Golden State Killer changed policing in America.

Within months, investigators across the country started using the same technique. It got a name: investigative genetic genealogy.

Cold cases that had been dead for decades suddenly had names. Killers caught after 30, 40, even 50 years. Unknown victims finally identified and returned to their families.

But it also raised hard questions. Millions of people had uploaded their DNA to find relatives, not to help police. Had they agreed to this?

After the case, GEDmatch changed its rules so users had to choose whether police could use their DNA.

Supporters say it brings justice to families who waited a lifetime. Critics say it turns every person who takes a DNA test into an informant on their entire family, without asking them.

Both sides agree on one thing. Without this method, Joseph James DeAngelo would probably have died a free man.

The debate about privacy is still going on.

So is everything about this case solved?

Legally, yes. He pleaded guilty and he will die in prison.

But some questions may never be answered. He has never explained why he did it. Why he started. Why he stopped in 1986. Investigators still wonder if there are crimes nobody ever connected to him.

And some families still don't know exactly what happened to the people they loved, in those last hours.

There's also the people who investigated him. Some detectives who worked the case in the 1970s died before the arrest. Others lived to sit in the courtroom and finally see his face.

Here's our view, based on the evidence.

The Golden State Killer wasn't caught by a confession, a witness or a mistake at a crime scene. He was caught because his DNA was waiting, preserved in evidence boxes for forty years, and because science finally caught up with him.

For decades, the man who terrified California mowed his lawn, fixed cars, and went shopping at the craft store. Like nothing had happened.

And the thing that caught him was the most ordinary thing in the world. The handle of his car door.

Here's our question for you. Should police be allowed to search public DNA websites to catch killers, even if it means using the DNA of innocent relatives? Tell us in the comments.

This is Vanished Files. Follow the channel for the next case file.
